newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mandela has mixed record as peacemaker.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mandela has mixed record as peacemaker.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela has had mixed success as Africa's foremost peace broker since he emerged in 1990 from a quarter century in jail to lead South Africa from apartheid to democracy.

His current bid to bring Zaire's rival leaders face-to-face in peace talks aboard a South African ship is the latest in a series of diplomatic initiatives based more on his own moral authority than his power.
Alone or in concert with other Southern African leaders, Mandela has contributed to peace-making missions in Angola, Algeria, Lesotho, Swaziland, Burundi, Zaire, Nigeria and Sudan.
But only in Lesotho, a tiny sovereign island within South Africa where he helped reverse a royal coup and prevent a military takeover, can he claim unequivocal success.
A Western diplomat told Reuters the international community hoped Mandela would be able to turn Africa towards stability, democracy and economic growth.

But he warned that, despite his immense moral stature, Mandela lacked experience and expertise because his 27 years of political imprisonment had spanned the most crucial phase of African decolonisation.
"President Mandela is always on the right side, but he can be naive and he is not immune to blunders," the diplomat said.

Mandela put his personal credibility on the line on Friday when he flew to Congo to personally escort Zaire's beleaguered Prsident Mobutu Sese Seko to his first direct encounter with rebel alliance leader Laurent Kabila.
He sent his heir apparent, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, to accompany Kabila to the ship cruising off the Atlantic coast.

If Mobutu and Kabila agree on a transition to democracy, Mandela, 78, will have scored his greatest triumph since his own country's peaceful transition three years ago from white minority rule to democracy.

That would be in sharp contrast to his failure to prevent the 1995 execution of Nigerian civil rights leader Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight associates or subsequently to win Western support for sanctions on the regime of military leader Sani Abacha.

Mandela had appealed personally to Abacha to spare Saro-Wiwa and arrange democratic elections and sent Mbeki, Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo and Nobel Peace Prize winner Archbishop Desmond Tutu on separate fruitless missions to Nigeria.
He has repeatedly criticised the United States and Europe for failing to use economic power to isolate Abacha and has backed a Commonwealth programme to bring Nigeria to democracy.

Three months later, in 1996, Mandela had to send Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad on a special mission to mend ruffled ties with Algerian President Liamine Zeroual. Mandela's policy is generally that he will listen to anyone, but he went too far for Zeroual when he met Algerian radical leader Anwar Haddam, branded a "terrorist mastermind".

Since then, Mandela has directed his peace-making largely through the Southern African Development Community linking South Africa and its immediate neighbours, through the United Nations or in collaboration with the Organisation of Afrian Unity.
Mandela has taken pains to consult regional leaders at every stage of his Zaire initiative to ensure he is not isolated as he was over Nigeria.
"He is spending a lot more time on regional issues this year than he has done in the past," said on official in his office.

"There are several initiatives under way in Africa at the moment, but they are all heading in one direction and they are in line with the president's concern for an African response to African problems."
